title: The lion's roar
hook: only here are the four kinds of noble ones, the Buddha roars (MN 11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta on right view, and your line, Sariputta teaches. Did you try his four questions on something that bothered you? Day four hundred ten.

A lion's roar isn't really a threat. It's an announcement: here I am, this is my ground, and I'm not afraid to say so. You can hear it for miles. Old Indian texts borrowed the phrase for a bold, unhedged claim, made out loud and in public. The Buddha's discourses contain several lion's roars, and two of them sit side by side in the Middle-Length Sayings. MN 11 is the shorter one. Today: the lion's roar.
screen: `HERE I AM.` → `THIS IS MY GROUND.` → `A CLAIM MADE OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: MN 11 is the Culasihanada, the shorter discourse on the lion's roar. The Buddha tells his monks that they may rightly roar: only here is there a first kind of noble one, a second, a third and a fourth. The commentaries read these as the four stages of awakening: the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner and the arahant. It's a strong claim, made in an age of open debate between many schools, each confident in its own teacher. What's interesting is what comes next. The Buddha expects that wanderers from other schools will ask: what's your basis for saying so? And he gives his monks an answer built from four things in their own lives: confidence in the Teacher, confidence in the teaching, the precepts fulfilled, and companions in the practice who are dear and agreeable. He then goes on to the question of clinging: to sense pleasures, to views, to rules and rituals, and to a doctrine of self, and says a teaching should make clear how each kind of clinging is understood. Notice the shape of it. The roar isn't volume. It isn't bravado. A lion roars because it knows its ground. You may remember the quail standing on its own clod a couple of weeks ago: same idea, louder. The confidence in this discourse rests on what the monks have actually lived: their trust, their practice, their friendships. A roar that rests on nothing is just noise.
screen: `SIHANADA — A BOLD CLAIM.` · `FOUR KINDS OF NOBLE ONES.` · `WHAT'S YOUR BASIS?` · `A LION KNOWS ITS GROUND.` · then, large: `A LION'S ROAR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and look for one thing you're actually sure of. Not something you've only been told, and not a grand claim about the universe. Something you've tested yourself: that a slow breath calms you, that a kind word lands better than a harsh one, that the post holds. Find it. Then, quietly, inside, say it once, plainly, with no maybe. Rest on it, the way the lion rests on its ground. The bell holds the time.
The lion's roar. Sihanada: a bold claim, made out loud, by someone who knows the ground they're standing on.
Your line: a lion's roar. Today, say one thing you've tested and are sure of, plainly, without hedging, to someone who'd want to hear it. Day four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Buddhists across schools use the lion's roar, sihanada, as an image for confident teaching, and the lion appears widely in Buddhist art; the four stages of awakening are central to Theravada teaching.

it means a confident declaration, made openly.

MN 11 is the only lion's roar in the Middle-Length Sayings
MN 12 is the greater lion's roar, told to Sariputta.

fork.setup: wanderers from another school ask the monks: what's your basis for that claim? what does MN 11 have them answer?
options: our teacher said so, and that's enough
confidence in Teacher and teaching, precepts kept, and dear companions
fork.reveal: four things the monks can find in their own lives: trust in the Teacher, trust in the teaching, the precepts fulfilled, and companions who are dear and agreeable.

original.note: Pali sīhanāda: a lion's roar; sīha is lion, nāda is sound.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lion's roar is a show of power.
what it means: a confident declaration made from ground you know.
what a scholar hears: sīhanāda names several suttas; MN 11 is the 'lesser' (cūḷa) lion's roar and MN 12 the 'greater' (mahā), told to Sāriputta.

notes: Sensitive day: MN 11's claim ('only here are the four kinds of noble ones') is about other schools of its time. The script reports it as the text's claim, set in an age of open debate, without endorsing it or comparing traditions today, and centers the day on the basis of confidence. A Keeper should check this framing.
The four noble ones as the four stages of awakening is the commentary's reading; stated as such.
The four kinds of clinging and the four grounds of confidence summarized from memory; please confirm.
